content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a method for interpretable continual learning.
The idea is to introduce two components, the basis models predicting $y$ from the input $x$, and the mixing network that determines the mixture weights of the basis models from the task feature $z$.
Moreover, by introducing an additional network estimating $z$ from $x$ and $y$, the entire model can adapt to new data without knowing the current task feature.
The authors claimed that by analyzing the latent representations of the estimated $z$, we can obtain some insights on the current task without knowing the true task feature, helping users to infer the similarity among the tasks.
The authors also proposed to add new basis models if none of the current basis model can fit the data well.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
I was not able to find any significant strength of the paper.

### Weakness
The essential weakness of the paper is that it misses an important prior study [Ref1].
The method of [Ref1] can do almost similar things considered in this paper.
That is, it can adapt to new tasks by using a subset of the existing models, add new structure to the model when it cannot fit the data, and it can infer the task when the task information is not available.
Moreover, all of these mechanisms are provided under a unified framework of variational Bayes and nonparameteric Bayes.
Although [Ref1] focuses on masking edges in DNNs, we can easily extend their framework to the mixture of multiple distinct models as considered in the current study by considering masks over models rather than edges.
The interpretability, or the similarity between the tasks, can be obtained by assessing the similarity of the masks as well.
To me, the current study looks like solving each subproblem individually which are already solved by [Ref1] under a unified Bayesian framework.
It would be essential to show the advantage of the proposed method over [Ref1] both in terms of methodological novelty as well as practical utility.

[Ref1] Bayesian Structural Adaptation for Continual Learning, ICML'21.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity, Quality, Novelty
The main idea of the paper is described clearly.
However, there is a problem on the discussion with related studies.
The authors only mention the meta-learning based continual learning methods.
Continual learning has several different types of approaches, and the current study needs to be positioned appropriately within that large literatures.

### Reproducibility
The authors provided detailed experiment setups in appendix.
The results will be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The problem of interpretable continual learning looks interesting and perhaps important in practice.
However, the novelty and the advantage of the proposed method is not well supported in the paper.
In particular, the paper only focuses on meta-learning based continual learning and misses other types of approaches including [Ref1] closely related to the current study.

content.summary_of_the_paper: It is proposed to use a mixture of basis for continual learning problem in regression settings. A basis is a single model, which is an ensemble itself in this work. There seem to be a very poor understanding of the literature of continual learning, claiming the approach to be novel when it is trivially known. Experimental validation is poor, only two baselines one of which is related to their approach itself. Figures are super hard to read, see Fig. 6 for instance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I don't see any strengths at all.


Weaknesses:
Purely incremental work, it may best serve an application paper for a workshop but not at ICLR.
No theoretical validation for the approach.
Experimental validation is poor, unclear, considering only two baselines. 
Poorly written.
Finance and weather domains are motivated in the introduction, but datasets for evaluation are completely different.


Some of the many papers which use the concept of mixture of experts are listed below. In the proposed approach, basis is nothing but a model in an ensemble.

Mixture-of-Variational-Experts for Continual Learning. 
A Neural Dirichlet Process Mixture Model for Task-Free Continual Learning.
Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing.
Meta-DMoE: Adapting to Domain Shift by Meta-Distillation from Mixture-of-Experts.
Learning an Evolved Mixture Model for Task-Free Continual Learning.
Task-Agnostic Online Reinforcement Learning with an Infinite Mixture of Gaussian Processes.
Continual Learning via Local Module Composition.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a continual learning algorithm in the setup of unknown task boundaries. It proposes to model each current task in the online stream as a mixture of basis models. These basis are pre-trained during an offline stage from a task-segmented dataset. Alternatively, they can be created in the offline and online stage, when current task is detected as `out of distribution` with respect to the task basis. For fast instantiation of new model basis the algorithm relies on MAML. To identify OOD tasks, the basis are constructed as ensembles allowing for estimation of variance. The authors experiment on multiple datasets documenting favourable performance of their method with respect to preduction accuracy, low number of needed basis and well structured latent space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strenght:
The paper addresses an important problem of continual learning through a novel approach that can attract the attention of the community. The experimental results show good performance compared to listed baselines.

Weknesses:
The paper is difficult to read and follow leaving me with multiple questions that I could not figure out from the text. Clarifying these better would greatly improve the paper.
Using the term "interpretable" in the title is misleading. The simple PCA-based analysis of the latent space does not, in my view, justify such a title. Model interpretability is an important concept gaining popularity but should not be used just for marketing purposes.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity of the paper could be increased. I have the following questions:
- Section 2 - you introduce the assumption of a Markovian task process. Why do you need it, where is it used?
- In section 3. you introduce the functions w as mapping z onto simplex. Is this just a softmax? If so, it would help the reader to simply state this. Otherwise please clarify how do you construct the map.
S
- Section 3.1 - at the end of the para after equation (2) you introduce $p_\theta(Z_t | Z_{t-1})$. Is this the same as $P_\theta(z_t | z_{t-1})$ above? If so, how can it be the iii) component of $P_\theta$, which is what the para says.
- Sectoin 3.1 you use $P_\Theta$ for both, the model distribuiton as well as the task transition prior. This is confusing.
- What is the distribution for $z_0$?
- How do you construct batches in the online setup - are these just 1 example? If bigger, can they contain a mix of multiple tasks?
- Pre-trained basis models: You say that empirically the basis models ended too similar. Can you provide any intuition as to why?
- $S_{ODDS}$ score is calculated over a single example in the online setup?
- When $b_{new}$ is instantiated from MAML, should not we expect that it is going to be always better than any other existing basis model? That would suggest that you shall be always OOD at every new example. I am probably missing something here.
- Equation 6 - please explain the nominator (and replace $M^{-1}$ with $1/M$. Like this it suggests some matrix inverse.
- Buffer of OOD examples - confusing. You evaluate the OOD property for every example but do not instantiate the new basis right away? What if the examples are OOD with respect to the existing basis but do not originate from the same task (according to your own definitions) so a single basis would not do for them?
- Figure 6 please correct the ordering and coloring in the last diagram to agree with the previous 3.

The paper is somewhat difficult to follow but overall the quality of the writing is satisfactory and the method seems sound.
As far as I know, while the method builds on existing concepts, the combination and the specific use is novel.
Reproducibility is limited - I didn't find any link to am existing codebase.
content.summary_of_the_review: Interesting paper addressing an important topic. The performance seems good. I recommend weak reject as there are multiple points that deserve clarifications. Also the title shall drop the "interpretable" term as I believe the paper does not sufficiently explore and address this topic and the term shall not be used just for marketing purposes.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles a continual learning setting in which access to partially labeled pre-training data is assumed. The proposed approach instantiates multiple neural network ensembles, both during the pre-training and the continual-learning phases, to tackle this setting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
STRENGTHS
- The paper and the proposed approach are very interesting.

WEAKNESSES
- The proposed approach is very niche and its practicality is somewhat limited. MoB requires pre-training data, an assumption which should not be taken for granted. Moreover, I am not sure if MoB would be able to work in a setting where the memory for storing models is limited.
- The experiments are very narrow. Most continual learning papers focus on classification or reinforcement learning experiments, but this paper only does regression, and I do not think this choice was sufficiently motivated.
- The paper does not adequately explain why MoB perform better than the other baselines. An interpretation of the results would be valuable, I think.
- Computational and memory complexity of MoB in comparison to baselines are not discussed. In Table 1, there is a comparison between the number of models that MoB and MOLe instantiate, but I do not view this comparison as fair, since each MoB model is an ensemble of neural networks. A more appropriate comparison would be the number of parameters of MoB and MOLe, for each benchmark.
- The paper does not explain why other approaches that do pre-training via meta-learning are not included in the evaluation (e.g., some of the ones discussed in Related Work, or for instance [1]).
- I found the description of MoB to be very short, especially when it comes to discussing Algorithms 1 and 2.

[1] Javed, K., & White, M. (2019). Meta-learning representations for continual learning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 32.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is relatively clear, but the technical aspects of the proposed approach (Algorithms 1 and 2) should have been discussed more extensively. To the best of my knowledge, MoB is novel, and I do not have any reason to doubt that the results of this paper are reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: Despite this paper being an interesting read, in its current form, it has a number of shortcomings.
